soil-phys-004.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs hold together?
soil-phys-004.text:
A soil can look healthy and still fall apart in the first hard rain. Soil aggregate stability measures how well aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage. It describes {{ref:soil-phys-001}}, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties.

It directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement. Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while meso- and macropores let water and air move in. Such soil usually takes in water faster and is not prone to ponding. In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients.

Clay, adsorbed calcium and magnesium, and iron oxides act as cementing agents, while exchangeable sodium lowers stability by promoting dispersion. Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors. Reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs improve aggregation, whereas heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower it. See also {{ref:soil-phys-005}}.

soil-phys-043.title: Specific surface area: why tiny grains do the most work
soil-phys-043.text: Surface is where soil does its chemistry. Specific surface area is the surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as area per unit mass. Surface area per unit weight rises as average particle size falls, so sand has the least and is least active, silt is intermediate and clay is the most active. Clay minerals form thin plates and typically have 10 to 1,000 square metres of surface per gram. In one table, very coarse sand (2.00-1.00 mm) has 90 particles per gram and 11 cm2/g, fine sand (0.25-0.10 mm) 46,000 and 91 cm2/g, and silt 5,776,000 and 454 cm2/g. That large surface, with many negative charges, gives clay its high capacity to retain water and nutrients, and the water held at field capacity depends on it. Particles of one textural class share properties tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as cation exchange capacity. One source instead describes it as the surface-area-to-volume ratio of particles.

soil-phys-249.title: Soil as solid, liquid and gas
soil-phys-249.text: Soil is never just dirt; it is three things at once. It combines solid, liquid and gas phases, and their interaction determines how it behaves. The solid phase is mineral particles (rocks, gravel, sand, silt, clay) or organic matter, and ideally takes up about 50% of the volume. The liquid phase is soil water plus dissolved nutrients, chemicals and gases, together forming the soil solution; both its quantity and its chemical composition matter. The gaseous phase is soil air, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide. Ideally it is about 25% of volume, but it is highly dynamic. Mass-volume relationships among the three phases define porosity, bulk density and the shares of water and air in pore space.

soil-phys-238.title: Critical state: when soil flows like a frictional fluid
soil-phys-238.text: Critical state soil mechanics is the branch of soil mechanics that models saturated remoulded soils on the critical state concept. At the critical state, stress and strain relate constantly: the soil keeps deforming without any further rise in stress, like a frictional fluid. In practice this marks failure. The concept was published in 1958 by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth, from Cambridge simple shear tests and Imperial College triaxial tests. The Cam-Clay models assume an isotropic, elasto-plastic soil with no creep, and the Modified Cam-Clay of John Burland uses an elliptical yield surface. It extends the ideas of {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and {{ref:soil-phys-073}}.

soil-phys-229.title: Three kinds of compaction and how to tell them apart
soil-phys-229.text:
Each kind of compaction has different signs and different remedies, so diagnosis comes first. Surface seals show broken-down aggregates, poor seedling emergence and fast runoff and erosion. Sandy loams and silt loams are especially prone, because their unstable aggregates leave small particles that fill pores into dense crusts.

Surface layer compaction shows as deep wheel tracks, standing water, cloddy tillage and stubby, crooked roots with few root hairs. A penetrometer, wire flag or shovel dig can confirm it. Freshly plowed soil can falsely look uncompacted because it is loose at first, while no-tilled soil is firmer but has strong structure and worm-made large pores.

Subsoil compaction is found with a penetrometer in field-moist soil, which often meets much higher resistance at the base of the plow layer (typically 6 to 8 inches), and by roots that are absent below the pan or run sideways above it. Compacted soil that stays wet becomes anaerobic, causing stunted growth and denitrification losses shown by yellow leaves. Weakened crops are more prone to root diseases such as Pythium and Fusarium. For background, see {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-233.title: Cover and rotation crops that loosen packed soil
soil-phys-233.text: Roots can do work that machines cannot. Cover and rotation crops reduce compaction by creating and stabilizing large voids and feeding microbes. Grasses have shallow dense roots that ease surface compaction but not subsoil, while deep taproots such as alfalfa and forage radish penetrate compacted subsoil, so mixes of shallow and deep rooters are often best. Perennial and cool-season crops have active early-season roots that reach compacted layers while still wet and soft. Clay soils stay plastic for long because the dry upper inch cuts evaporation; a spring cereal rye cover pumps water from below and helps the soil pass from plastic to friable, instead of fall tillage. Plowing down a crop loosens trafficked soil and speeds nitrogen mineralization, whereas cutting and mulching in no-till gives weed control and better infiltration but does not loosen the soil. This answers {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-236.title: Managing field traffic to spare the soil
soil-phys-236.text: Most compaction is avoidable if the right passes are changed. Judge traffic by soil moisture at the time and by equipment weight and load distribution. Late dry planting does little damage, but wet-harvest trucks and spring plowing of wet clay loam do much. Tracks greatly reduce subsoil compaction. Multiple axles, and wide tires at low inflation pressure, spread loads, and most compaction comes from the first tire passing. Dual wheels enlarge the footprint but cut subsoil compaction less, because pressure cones merge at shallow depth, and they tempt fieldwork on wet soil. Poorly drained fields suffer worse compaction; tile drainage dries the subsoil, and surface shaping and mole drains suit heavy clay. The problem itself is in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-232.title: How organic matter helps soil resist compaction
soil-phys-232.text: Organic matter protects soil in several ways at once. It covers everything from living roots to well-decomposed material. Surface residue dissipates the compacting force of equipment, and organic matter is less dense than mineral particles. Dead residue and organisms stabilize aggregates, while roots and large organisms create channels for air and water. Roots and mycorrhizal fungi secrete sticky substances that bind small aggregates into larger ones. One caution: heavy manure spreaders on wet soil can severely compact surface and subsoil, so organic materials should be applied without worsening compaction. The risk it guards against is {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-239.title: The headland: the most trampled part of a field
soil-phys-239.text: The ends of a field take a beating. A headland is the area at each end of a planted field, used for turning implements. It gets more traffic per unit area than the rest of the field, so its soil is more compacted and yields are generally lower. Fertility is often higher there, because overlapping fertilizer applications coincide with reduced yields.

soil-phys-237.title: Dynamic compaction: dropping tonnes to densify ground
soil-phys-237.text: Weights of 8 to 36 tonnes are dropped from 1 to 30 metres, and the stress waves can reach up to 10 metres deep. Dynamic compaction is a ground improvement method that densifies soil by repeatedly dropping a heavy weight at regularly spaced points. In cohesionless soils the waves cause liquefaction followed by compaction; in cohesive soils they raise {{ref:soil-phys-098}} before compaction. Results depend on weight, drop height and spacing. Old fills and granular soils are most often treated, and soil below the water table needs care to let excess pore pressure escape. It is an engineered form of {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-230.title: Crops that compact soil and how to offset them
soil-phys-230.text: Some crops are hard on soil. Root and tuber crops, silage corn, soybeans and many vegetable crops compact it through intensive tillage, low residue return or wet-soil harvest traffic. Countermeasures include soil-improving rotation crops, extensive cover crops, controlled traffic and extra manure or compost. In an 11-year Vermont trial on clay soil under continuous corn silage, yearly dairy manure of 0, 10, 20 and 30 tons per acre gave pore space of 44%, 45%, 47% and 50% of soil volume.

soil-phys-234.title: Deep tillage: breaking up a plow pan
soil-phys-234.text: Deeper tillage shatters a plow pan or other deep compacted layer so roots can explore deeper. It must be done when the full depth is dry and friable, otherwise it smears the soil. Subsoiling below the 6 to 8 inch depth of normal tillage is costly and energy consuming, and does little for surface compaction from aggregate breakdown; narrow-shank zone building or deep strip tillage disturbs less. It works better on coarse soils, because in fine soils the whole subsoil is strong, and tilling wet subsoil can cause smearing and drainage problems. Heavy loads must stay off afterwards to prevent re-compaction, and soils prone to washed-down fines may need repeated deep tillage.

soil-phys-235.title: Loosening soil without a full plow
soil-phys-235.text: Some tools loosen compacted soil with only minor surface disturbance, helping a tilled field move toward no-till. Aerators with rotating tines give shallow relief in dense surface layers and can incorporate manure with little tillage damage. Strip tillage, 6 to 8 inches deep with narrow shanks, disturbs soil only where plant rows will be and promotes rooting; yeoman's plows act similarly with almost no surface disturbance. Patience is needed, though. Compacted soils become addicted to tillage, so switching to no-till at once may fail. No-till benefits usually take 2 to 5 years, faster with cover crops.
